title: The futur simple
topic: formation and uses of the future; quand + future; si + present + future
why: This lesson opens the unit on plans with the futur simple: its single set of endings, its irregular stems, and how it differs from aller + infinitive. It also tackles the classic trap of quand + future, where English uses the present, and si + present + future.

Will: the futur simple

English builds the future with a helper word: \"I will speak\". French builds it in a single word, by adding endings to the infinitive: je parlerai. The endings are the same for every verb, and they look like the present of avoir (ai, as, a, avons, avez, ont), minus the av- in nous and vous.

parlerfinirprendre
jeparleraifiniraiprendrai
tuparlerasfinirasprendras
il / elle / onparlerafiniraprendra
nousparleronsfinironsprendrons
vousparlerezfinirezprendrez
ils / ellesparlerontfinirontprendront

-re verbs drop their final e before the ending: prendre → je prendrai, attendre → j'attendrai. The future always has an r before the ending: that r is how you recognize it.

Verbs with a spelling change keep it in every form: acheter → j'achèterai, appeler → j'appellerai, se lever → je me lèverai.

L'année prochaine, je travaillerai à Lyon.Next year, I'll work in Lyon.
Nous partirons en juillet et nous rentrerons en août.We'll leave in July and come back in August.

Pronunciation: in everyday speech, the e of parlerai often disappears: « parl'rai », « j'achèt'rai ». And the -ai of je parlerai sounds like é.

", "

Irregular stems

The most frequent verbs have an irregular stem, but the endings never change. Learn the stems in groups:

InfinitiveFutureInfinitiveFuture
êtreje seraipouvoirje pourrai
avoirj'auraivoirje verrai
allerj'iraienvoyerj'enverrai
faireje feraivouloirje voudrai
savoirje sauraivenirje viendrai
devoirje devraifalloiril faudra
pleuvoiril pleuvra

Notice the double rr in pourrai, verrai, enverrai: you hear a longer r. And aller becomes a tiny ir-: j'irai, tu iras, nous irons.

Futur simple or aller + infinitive?

You already know the near future: Je vais partir. Both talk about the future, but the feeling is different:

  • aller + infinitive: something close, planned or already under way: Attention, tu vas tomber !, Ce soir, je vais dîner chez Léa.
  • futur simple: predictions, promises, longer-term plans, things less certain: Un jour, j'habiterai près de la mer., Je t'appellerai, promis !

The weather forecast

The forecast is a classic use of the future:

Demain, il fera beau dans le Sud, mais il pleuvra en Bretagne. Le soir, il y aura du vent.Tomorrow, it will be sunny in the South, but it will rain in Brittany. In the evening, it will be windy.

Il y a becomes il y aura (there will be), and il faut becomes il faudra (it will be necessary / we'll have to).

", "

Quand + future, si + present

This is the big trap for English speakers. In English, after \"when\" and \"as soon as\" you use the present for a future action: \"When I get to Paris, I'll call you\". French is logical: if the action is in the future, the verb is in the future.

Quand je serai à Paris, je t'appellerai.When I'm in Paris, I'll call you.
Dès que j'aurai les billets, je te les enverrai.As soon as I have the tickets, I'll send them to you.

Never Quand je suis à Paris, je t'appellerai: that mixes two time frames.

But si + present

After si (if), it's the other way round: si is followed by the present, and the result is in the future. Here, French works exactly like English.

si + presentfuture
S'il fait beau,on ira à la plage.
Si tu as le temps,tu viendras avec nous ?
Si vous prenez le train de huit heures,vous arriverez à midi.

Never put the future after si: « si il fera beau » is a mistake twice over. Si elides only before il and ils: s'il, s'ils, but si elle, si on.

Resolutions

L'année prochaine, je ferai du sport, j'arrêterai de fumer et je lirai un livre par mois.Next year, I'll exercise, I'll quit smoking and I'll read a book a month.

A memory trick: quand looks to the future, so it takes the future; si is a condition, so it takes the present.
